# Data

## Sources

Our primary data source is the **Swiss Household Panel (SHP)**, *Living in Switzerland Waves 1–26 + Long file + Beta version Wave 27*, Version 12.0, published by FORS and distributed through SWISSUbase [@shp2026]. The version-specific dataset DOI is [10.48573/haxy-c230](https://doi.org/10.48573/haxy-c230); the canonical DOI is [10.48573/pjmf-8s41](https://doi.org/10.48573/pjmf-8s41). Access for this educational research project was approved on **19 October 2026**. We used the SAS files from the release, excluding the beta Wave 27.

Although the release contains waves dating back to 1999, our analysis covers **2004–2024 (21 annual waves)** because the general job-satisfaction measure is unavailable in several earlier years. We combined annual individual and household records to study employed respondents across Switzerland. The underlying microdata are access-controlled; we do not redistribute them with the report.

## Description

Our preparation process produced three related datasets:

| Dataset | Respondent-year observations | Unique respondents | Purpose |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Full dataset | 305,462 | 45,632 | Harmonised individual and household records |
| Employed sample | 124,769 | 22,265 | Employed respondents with valid occupation and job satisfaction |
| Analysis sample | 124,766 | — | Employed sample excluding missing age or sex |

The **full dataset has 10 standardised variables**: `IDPERS` (respondent identifier), `IDHOUS` (household identifier), `YEAR`, `AGE`, `SEX`, `EMPLOYMENT_STATUS`, `WORKING_STATUS`, `OCCUPATION`, `JOB_SATISFACTION` and `REGION`. Job satisfaction is measured on a **0–10 scale**; occupation is grouped using ISCO major groups; `REGION` describes **region of residence**, not necessarily the region of employment. Employment arrangements are analysed separately from the employment-status filter.

Each row represents a respondent in a particular survey year. Since individuals can appear in multiple waves, the number of rows is larger than the number of distinct respondents. The sample also varies across years and occupational groups, which matters when comparing means.

## Loading Data

We initially read annual SAS files using Python and `pyreadstat`, selected the relevant columns and merged individual and household information. We then saved the harmonised datasets as CSV files under `data/processed/`, so the report can use the prepared data without rerunning the entire raw-data pipeline [@mckinney2022python; @pandasdocs].

The following chunk loads the processed files using paths relative to the project root. It requires the three CSV files exported by `01_data_preparation.ipynb` to be present in `data/processed/`.

```{python}
#| label: load-data
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display
from pathlib import Path

project_root = Path.cwd().resolve()

if not (project_root / "data" / "processed").is_dir():
    project_root = project_root.parent

processed_dir = project_root / "data" / "processed"
full_dataset = pd.read_csv(processed_dir / "full_dataset.csv")
employed_sample = pd.read_csv(processed_dir / "employed_sample.csv")
analysis_sample = pd.read_csv(processed_dir / "analysis_sample.csv")

sample_overview = pd.DataFrame({
    "Dataset": ["Full dataset", "Employed sample", "Analysis sample"],
    "Observations": [len(full_dataset), len(employed_sample), len(analysis_sample)],
    "Variables": [full_dataset.shape[1], employed_sample.shape[1], analysis_sample.shape[1]],
})
display(sample_overview)
```

## Wrangling

### General Transformations

We first inspected the available variables and their coding in the annual SHP files, testing the preparation procedure on individual waves before automating it for **2004–2024**. For each wave, we selected the relevant individual and household variables, converted invalid survey codes to missing values, harmonised column names, merged the files using their appropriate identifiers and added the survey year. The annual datasets were then concatenated into a single dataset.

For the employed sample, we retained respondents with **`WORKING_STATUS == 1`**, a valid occupation code (ISCO major groups 0–9) and a job-satisfaction score from 0 to 10. We did **not** use `EMPLOYMENT_STATUS` as the employment filter: that variable is retained for comparisons of employment arrangements. The smaller analysis sample additionally excludes the **two missing age values and one missing sex value** in the employed sample. For some regressions, further complete-case restrictions apply; their sample sizes are reported in the Analysis section.

### Spotting Mistakes and Missing Data

We checked identifiers, survey-year coverage, duplicates and missing values after combining the annual files. The full dataset contains **no duplicate respondent-year combinations**, and respondent ID, survey year, household ID and region are complete.

| Variable | Missing observations in full dataset |
|---|---:|
| Age | 232 |
| Sex | 4 |
| Employment status | 1,003 |
| Occupation | 180,252 |
| Job satisfaction | 178,161 |

The high missingness in occupation and job satisfaction partly reflects the inclusion of non-employed respondents in the full dataset. Rather than imputing these central research variables, we restrict the employed sample to observations with valid occupation and job-satisfaction values. This ensures the outcomes and occupational categories being compared are observed, although exclusions may affect representativeness.

### Listing Anomalies and Outliers

We checked the survey's special missing-value codes and the permitted ranges of key variables. **Valid job-satisfaction scores from 0 to 10 were retained**, including low and high responses; these are meaningful values rather than outliers to remove. The Armed Forces occupation group (ISCO 0) is present but small (**131 observations** in the demographic analysis sample), so it is excluded from the civilian-occupation regressions and some comparative figures. We also checked for duplicate respondent-year records and found none.

### Survey Weights and Comparability

The SHP provides annual individual cross-sectional survey weights for all 21 analysed years. We matched these to the employed sample by respondent ID and year. **121,547 of 124,769 observations (97.42%)** have positive weights; **3,222** have zero or negative weight codes and were excluded from weighted calculations.

| Annual mean job satisfaction | 2004 | 2024 | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Unweighted | 8.212 | 7.815 | −0.397 |
| Weighted | 8.207 | 7.711 | −0.496 |

Both comparisons indicate a decline over the period. We retain unweighted results for the main exploratory analysis and use weighted annual means as a robustness comparison. The weights were not adjusted specifically for the employed subgroup, and these calculations do not implement the full complex survey design. Similarly, repeated observations of the same respondents require care in formal statistical testing; the preliminary regressions use respondent-clustered standard errors.

The complete data preparation and validation code is retained in `01_data_preparation.ipynb`; this update report presents the essential decisions and checks rather than reproducing every processing step.
